claim: Nanos RNA-binding proteins are required for germline development in metazoans.
source: Nanos RNA-binding proteins are required for germline development in metazoans, but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a general statement about Nanos proteins supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: nos-1nos-2 PGCs fail to silence hundreds of transcripts normally expressed in oocytes.
source: nos-1nos-2 PGCs fail to silence hundreds of transcripts normally expressed in oocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Misregulation in nos-1nos-2 PGCs is due to both delayed turnover of maternal transcripts and inappropriate transcriptional activation.
source: We find that this misregulation is due to both delayed turnover of maternal transcripts and inappropriate transcriptional activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing embryonic and L1 PGCs and in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: Inappropriate transcriptional activation in nos-1nos-2 PGCs is an indirect consequence of delayed turnover of the maternally-inherited transcription factor LIN-15B.
source: The latter appears to be an indirect consequence of delayed turnover of the maternally-inherited transcription factor LIN-15B, a synMuvB class transcription factor known to antagonize PRC2 activity.
evidence: This is supported by genetic suppression experiments and transcriptome analysis.

claim: LIN-15B is a synMuvB class transcription factor known to antagonize PRC2 activity.
source: The latter appears to be an indirect consequence of delayed turnover of the maternally-inherited transcription factor LIN-15B, a synMuvB class transcription factor known to antagonize PRC2 activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PRC2 is required for chromatin reprogramming in the germline.
source: PRC2 is required for chromatin reprogramming in the germline, and the transcriptome of PGCs lacking PRC2 resembles that of nos-1nos-2 PGCs.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of transcriptomes and established knowledge about PRC2 function.

claim: The transcriptome of PGCs lacking PRC2 resembles that of nos-1nos-2 PGCs.
source: PRC2 is required for chromatin reprogramming in the germline, and the transcriptome of PGCs lacking PRC2 resembles that of nos-1nos-2 PGCs.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing mes-2, mes-4, and nos-1nos-2 mutants.

claim: Loss of maternal LIN-15B restores fertility to nos-1nos-2 mutants.
source: Loss of maternal LIN-15B restores fertility to nos-1nos-2 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by genetic crosses and sterility counts.

claim: Nanos promotes germ cell fate by downregulating maternal RNAs and proteins that would otherwise interfere with PRC2-dependent reprogramming of PGC chromatin.
source: These findings suggest that Nanos promotes germ cell fate by downregulating maternal RNAs and proteins that would otherwise interfere with PRC2-dependent reprogramming of PGC chromatin.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental data presented.

claim: In mice, the transcriptional repressor BLIMP1 initiates PGC specification by blocking the expression of a mesodermal program active in neighboring somatic cells.
source: For example, in mice, the transcriptional repressor BLIMP1 initiates PGC specification by blocking the expression of a mesodermal program active in neighboring somatic cells (Ohinata et al., 2005; Saitou et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In C. elegans, the NSD methyltransferase MES-4 and the Polycomb Repressive Complex (PRC2, including MES-2, 3 and 6) cooperate to place active and repressive histone marks on germline and somatic genes, respectively.
source: In C. elegans, the NSD methyltransferase MES-4 and the Polycomb Repressive Complex (PRC2, including MES-2, 3 and 6) cooperate to place active and repressive histone marks on germline and somatic genes, respectively (Gaydos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: BLIMP1 and MES/PRC2 chromatin regulators are not germline-specific factors and also function during the differentiation of somatic lineages.
source: Despite their critical roles during germ cell development, the BLIMP1 and MES/PRC2 chromatin regulators are not germline-specific factors and also function during the differentiation of somatic lineages (Cui et al., 2006; Gaydos et al., 2012; Seydoux and Braun, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Components of the DRM class of transcriptional regulators and LIN-15B have been implicated in the silencing of germline genes in somatic cells.
source: Among these, components of the DRM (named for its Dp/E2F, pRB, and MuvB subunits) class of transcriptional regulators and LIN-15B, a THAP domain DNA binding protein, have been implicated in the silencing of germline genes in somatic cells (Petrella et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Loss of DRM factors or LIN-15B causes ectopic activation of germline genes in somatic cells leading to growth arrest at elevated temperatures (26°C).
source: Loss of DRM factors or LIN-15B causes ectopic activation of germline genes in somatic cells leading to growth arrest at elevated temperatures (26°C).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge from previous genetic studies.

claim: Inactivation of mes-2, mes-3, mes-4 and mes-6 suppresses the ectopic germline gene expression and restores viability to lin-15B mutants at 26°C.
source: Inactivation of mes-2, mes-3, mes-4 and mes-6 suppresses the ectopic germline gene expression and restores viability to lin-15B mutants at 26°C (Petrella et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DRM factors and LIN-15B antagonize MES activity in somatic lineages to keep germline genes off.
source: These observations have suggested that DRM factors and LIN-15B antagonizes MES activity in somatic lineages to keep germline genes off (Petrella et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference from previous genetic studies cited.

claim: Reducing the function of the synMuvB transcription factor lin-54 in mes-4 mutants restores the expression of X-linked genes closer to wild-type levels.
source: Reducing the function of the synMuvB transcription factor lin-54 in mes-4 mutants restores the expression of X-linked genes closer to wild-type levels (Tabuchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In the germline, MES activity antagonizes DRM activity to keep the X chromosome silent.
source: Therefore in the germline, MES activity antagonizes DRM activity to keep the X chromosome silent.
evidence: This is an inference from genetic studies cited.

claim: Competition between the MES chromatin modifiers and the DRM/LIN-15B transcription factors balances the transcription of somatic and germline genes in somatic and germline tissues.
source: Together, these genetic studies suggest that competition between the MES chromatin modifiers and the DRM/LIN-15B transcription factors balance the transcription of somatic and germline genes in somatic and germline tissues.
evidence: This is an inference from multiple genetic studies.

claim: The zygote inherits from the oocyte maternal mRNAs that promote the development of somatic and germline cell fates during embryogenesis.
source: The zygote (stripped red and green) inherits from the oocyte maternal mRNAs that promote the development of somatic (red) and germline (green) cell fates during embryogenesis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and is established knowledge.

claim: P4 is the germline founder cell that gives rise to Z2 and Z3, the two primordial germ cells.
source: P4 is the germline founder cell that gives rise to Z2 and Z3, the two primordial germ cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: Z2 and Z3 do not divide and remain mostly transcriptionally quiescent during embryogenesis.
source: Z2 and Z3 do not divide and remain mostly transcriptionally quiescent during embryogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans PGC development.

claim: Z2 and Z3 resume division and transcription in the first larval stage (L1).
source: They resume division and transcription in the first larval stage (L1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans PGC development.

claim: 461 transcripts were underexpressed in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs compared to wild-type.
source: These analyses identified 461 underexpressed transcripts and 871 overexpressed transcripts in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs compared to wild-type (q < 0.05, Figure 1C and Supplementary file 5 for list of misregulated genes).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 871 transcripts were overexpressed in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs compared to wild-type.
source: These analyses identified 461 underexpressed transcripts and 871 overexpressed transcripts in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs compared to wild-type (q < 0.05, Figure 1C and Supplementary file 5 for list of misregulated genes).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 31% (144/461) of underexpressed transcripts in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs correspond to genes expressed preferentially in pregametic germ cells.
source: We found that 31% (144/461) of underexpressed transcripts in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs correspond to genes expressed preferentially in pregametic germ cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The sygl-1 transcript was decreased by 4.7-fold in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs.
source: The sygl-1 transcript was decreased by 4.7-fold in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Overexpressed transcripts in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs correspond primarily to genes expressed in oocytes (380/871).
source: In contrast, overexpressed transcripts in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs correspond primarily to genes expressed in oocytes (380/871) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The lin-41 transcript was upregulated 5.1-fold in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs.
source: The lin-41, tbx-2, and hnd-1 transcripts were upregulated 5.1-fold, 11-fold and 91-fold, respectively, in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The tbx-2 transcript was upregulated 11-fold in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs.
source: The lin-41, tbx-2, and hnd-1 transcripts were upregulated 5.1-fold, 11-fold and 91-fold, respectively, in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The hnd-1 transcript was upregulated 91-fold in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs.
source: The lin-41, tbx-2, and hnd-1 transcripts were upregulated 5.1-fold, 11-fold and 91-fold, respectively, in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs overexpress oogenic and maternal genes normally expressed in oocytes, and fail to activate pregametic genes normally expressed in PGCs.
source: We conclude that nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs overexpress oogenic and maternal genes normally expressed in oocytes, and fail to activate pregametic genes normally expressed in PGCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The transcriptome of EMB PGCs consists primarily of maternal mRNAs inherited from the oocyte.
source: By comparing the EMB PGC transcriptome to a published oocyte transcriptome (Stoeckius et al., 2014), we observed an excellent correlation in relative transcript abundance between oocytes and EMB PGCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the transcriptome of EMB PGCs consists primarily of maternal mRNAs inherited from the oocyte.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 411 transcripts were down-regulated during the transition from EMB PGCs to L1 PGCs in wild-type, including 197 oocyte transcripts.
source: We identified 411 down-regulated transcripts, including 197 oocyte transcripts (Figure 2A and B and Supplementary file 5), consistent with turnover of many maternal mRNAs in PGCs after the 200 cell stage.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The amplitude of maternal mRNA turnover was diminished in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) mutants during the transition from EMB PGCs to L1 PGCs.
source: Strikingly, the amplitude of this turnover was diminished in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) mutants: the abundance of the 411 transcripts remained high overall during the transition from EMB PGCs to L1 PGCs in nos-2(RNAi)nos-1(gv5) embryos (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 182 transcripts were differentially expressed when comparing wild type and nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) EMB PGCs (11 down- and 171 upregulated), including 71 oocyte transcripts that were more abundant in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) EMB PGCs.
source: Furthermore, when comparing wild type and nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) EMB PGCs, we identified 182 differentially expressed transcripts (11 down- and 171 upregulated), including 71 of oocyte transcripts that were more abundant in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) EMB PGCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is a defect in maternal mRNA turnover in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs that is already detectable at the 200 cell stage and persists through embryogenesis.
source: Together these findings suggest a defect in maternal mRNA turnover in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs that is already detectable at the 200 cell stage and persists through embryogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference from the RNA-seq data comparing embryonic and L1 PGCs.

claim: In wild-type embryos, mex-5, C01G8.1 and Y51F10.2 are turned over rapidly in somatic lineages (before the 28 cell stage) and more slowly in the germ lineage (200–300 cell stage for mex-5 and C01G8.1; bean-stage for Y51F10.2).
source: In wild-type embryos, mex-5, C01G8.1 and Y51F10.2 are turned over rapidly in somatic lineages (before the 28 cell stage) and more slowly in the germ lineage (200–300 cell stage for mex-5 and C01G8.1; bean-stage for Y51F10.2).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: In nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) embryos, turnover of mex-5, C01G8.1 and Y51F10.2 was not affected in somatic lineages, but was delayed in PGCs.
source: We found that, in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) embryos, turnover was not affected in somatic lineages, but was delayed in PGCs, with C01G8.1 and mex-5 persisting to the ~500 cell stage and Y51F10.2 persisting to 1.5-fold stage (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Turnover of maternal mRNAs is compromised in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs.
source: We conclude that turnover of maternal mRNAs is compromised in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in situ hybridization and RNA-seq data.

claim: 130 transcripts increased in abundance during the transition from EMB to L1 PGCs in wild-type, including 30% (39/130) in the pregamete category.
source: We identified 130 such transcripts in wild-type PGCs, including 30% in the pregamete category (39/130, Figure 2B), consistent with PGCs transitioning to a pregamete fate by the L1 stage.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs, 510 transcripts increased in abundance during embryogenesis, distributed among all gene categories, including oocyte genes (16%, 84/510).
source: In contrast, in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs, many more (510) transcripts increased in abundance during embryogenesis, and these were distributed among all genes categories, including oocyte genes (16%, 84/510 Figure 2E and F and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs fail to transition to a pregamete program and instead adopt a hybrid transcriptional profile that includes activation of oocyte genes.
source: This finding suggests that, unlike wild-type PGCs, nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs fail to transition to a pregamete program and instead adopt a hybrid transcriptional profile that includes activation of oocyte genes.
evidence: This is an inference from the RNA-seq data.

claim: 221 genes showed increased chromatin accessibility at their promoter region in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs compared to wild-type.
source: We identified 221 genes that showed increased chromatin accessibility at their promoter region in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs compared to wild-type ('ATAC-seq+' genes; Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Most of the ATAC-seq+ genes were overexpressed in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs compared to wild-type.
source: Consistent with transcriptional activation, most of the ATAC-seq+ genes were overexpressed in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs compared to wild-type (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 108/221 of the ATAC-seq+ genes were oocyte genes.
source: Furthermore, 108/221 of the ATAC-seq +genes were oocyte genes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 29 genes showed decreased chromatin accessibility in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) compared to wild-type, most of which (13/29) were in the pregametic category.
source: In contrast, we identified 29 genes with decreased chromatin accessibility in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) compared to wild-type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2), most of which (13/29) were in the pregametic category (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: nos-1nos-2 PGCs fail to fully activate the transcription of pregamete genes and instead activate many oocyte genes.
source: These observations confirm that nos-1nos-2 PGCs fail to fully activate the transcription of pregamete genes and instead activate many oocyte genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: 63% (139/221) of the ATAC-seq+ genes were X-linked.
source: Strikingly, 63% (139/221) of the ATAC-seq+ genes were X-linked (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Transcripts from X-linked genes are rare in wild-type L1 PGCs (average 4.7 FPKM per X-linked genes compared to 50.9 for autosomal genes).
source: Furthermore, we found that, while transcripts from X-linked genes are rare in wild-type L1 PGCs (average 4.7 FPKM per X-linked genes compared to 50.9 for autosomal genes), they are more abundant in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs (9.6 FPKM for X-linked genes compared to 43.8 for autosomal genes) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: X-linked transcripts are more abundant in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs (9.6 FPKM for X-linked genes compared to 43.8 for autosomal genes).
source: Furthermore, we found that, while transcripts from X-linked genes are rare in wild-type L1 PGCs (average 4.7 FPKM per X-linked genes compared to 50.9 for autosomal genes), they are more abundant in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs (9.6 FPKM for X-linked genes compared to 43.8 for autosomal genes) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Silencing of the X chromosome is defective in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs, consistent with these cells adopting an oocyte-like transcriptional profile.
source: We conclude that silencing of the X chromosome is defective in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs, consistent with these cells adopting an oocyte-like transcriptional profile.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data.

claim: Failure to silence X-linked genes has been reported for germ cells lacking the chromatin regulators mes-2 and mes-4.
source: Failure to silence X-linked genes has been reported for germ cells lacking the chromatin regulators mes-2 and mes-4 (Bender et al., 2006; Gaydos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of mes-2 and mes-4 led to a significant upregulation of X-linked genes in L1 PGCs.
source: As expected, loss of mes-2 and mes-4 led to a significant upregulation of X-linked genes in L1 PGCs (Figure 4A–B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 5 for lists of misregulated genes).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between mes-2 and mes-4 for X-linked genes (R = 0.91) and autosomal oocyte genes (R = 0.76).
source: As expected, we observed a strong positive correlation between mes-2 and mes-4 in both gene categories (R = 0.91 and R = 0.76, X-linked and autosomal oocyte genes, respectively) (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: There is a strong correlation between mes-4(RNAi) and nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) for X-linked genes (R = 0.75).
source: We also observed a strong correlation between mes-4(RNAi) and nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) (R = 0.75, Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and mes-2(RNAi) and nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) (R = 0.73, not shown) for X-linked genes.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The correlation between mes-4(RNAi) and nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) is weaker for autosomal oocyte genes (R = 0.35).
source: Interestingly, the correlations were weaker for autosomal oocyte genes (R = 0.35, Figure 4F), which tended to be more overexpressed in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: nos-1nos-2 and mes PGCs share a defect in the silencing of X-linked loci, but nos-1nos-2 PGCs also have an additional defect in maternal mRNA turnover.
source: This finding is consistent with the notion that, while nos-1nos-2 and mes PGCs share a defect in the silencing of X-linked loci, nos-1nos-2 PGCs also have an additional defect in maternal mRNA turn over.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: No significant changes in mes transcripts were observed in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs compared to wild-type.
source: We observed no significant changes in mes transcripts in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs compared to wild-type (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: MES-2, MES-3 and MES-4 protein expression patterns were unchanged in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) or nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) embryos.
source: Direct examination of MES-2, MES-3 and MES-4 proteins confirmed that their expression patterns were unchanged in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) or nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: nos-1 and nos-2 do not affect MES expression despite being required for MES-dependent silencing.
source: Together, these results suggest that nos-1 and nos-2 do not affect MES expression despite being required for MES-dependent silencing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from RNA-seq and immunostaining data.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in lin-15B, lin-35 and dpl-1 reduced the sterility of nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) from >70% to <30%.
source: We found that loss-of-function mutations in lin-15B, lin-35 and dpl-1 reduced the sterility of nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) from >70% to<30%. (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: lin-15B(n744) reduced nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) sterility to 3.4%.
source: The most dramatic reduction was seen with lin-15B(n744), which reduced nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) sterility to 3.4% (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Other DRM components (efl-1, lin-37, lin-9, lin-52, lin-54) did not suppress nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) sterility.
source: Other DRM components (efl-1, lin-37, lin-9, lin-52, lin-54), however, did not suppress nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) sterility (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: lin-15B(n744) suppressed mes-2(ok2480) and mes-4(ok2326) sterility weakly and only for one generation.
source: We found that lin-15B(n744) suppressed mes-2(ok2480) and mes-4(ok2326) sterility weakly and only for one generation.
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis.

claim: Animals derived from mes-2(ok2480);lin-15B(n744) mothers were 83% sterile in the first generation and 98% sterile in the second generation and could not be maintained as a selfing population.
source: Animals derived from mes-2(ok2480);lin-15B(n744) mothers were 83% sterile in the first generation and 98% sterile in the second generation and could not be maintained as a selfing population (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103); lin-15B(n744) triple mutant animals were almost fully fertile (96.6% fertile) and could be maintained as a selfing population for >10 generations.
source: In contrast, nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103); lin-15B(n744) triple mutant animals were almost fully fertile (96.6% fertile, Figure 5A) and could be maintained as a selfing population for >10 generations.
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The fertility of nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103);lin-15B(n744) hermaphrodites was dependent on mes activity.
source: The fertility of nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103);lin-15B(n744) hermaphrodites was dependent on mes activity: inactivation by RNAi of mes-2 or mes-4 in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103);lin-15B resulted in 100% sterility (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The sterility of nos-1nos-2 mutants is due, at least in part, to inappropriate inhibition of MES function in PGCs by LIN-15B.
source: These genetic observations suggest that the sterility of nos-1nos-2 mutants is due, at least in part to, inappropriate inhibition of MES function in PGCs by LIN-15B.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic suppression experiments.

claim: LIN-15B expression was first detected in the germline in the L4 stage in nuclei near the end of the pachytene region where germ cells initiate oogenesis.
source: We first detected LIN-15B expression in the germline in the L4 stage in nuclei near the end of the pachytene region where germ cells initiate oogenesis (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Nuclear LIN-15B was present in all oocytes and inherited by all embryonic blastomeres, including the germline P blastomeres.
source: Nuclear LIN-15B was present in all oocytes and inherited by all embryonic blastomeres, including the germline P blastomeres (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: LIN-15B remained present at high levels in all somatic nuclei throughout embryogenesis.
source: LIN-15B remained present at high levels in all somatic nuclei throughout embryogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining observations.

claim: In the germ lineage, LIN-15B levels decreased sharply during the division of the germline founder cell P4 that generates the two PGCs.
source: In contrast, in the germ lineage, LIN-15B levels decreased sharply during the division of the germline founder cell P4 that generates the two PGCs (Figure 6B Left panels).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: LIN-15B expression remained at background levels in PGCs throughout embryogenesis.
source: LIN-15B expression remained at background levels in PGCs throughout embryogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining observations.

claim: lin-15B transcripts were modestly elevated in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) EMB PGCs compared to wild-type EMB PGCs.
source: lin-15B transcripts were modestly elevated in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) EMB PGCs compared to wild-type EMB PGCs, suggesting that lin-15B may be one of the maternal RNAs that requires Nanos activity for rapid turnover in PGCs (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: lin-15B transcript levels rose by ~2 fold in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) embryos during the transition from EMB to L1 PGCs but not in wild-type embryos.
source: During the transition from EMB to L1 PGCs, lin-15B transcript levels rose by ~2 fold in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) embryos but not in wild-type embryos, suggesting that the lin-15B locus is also inappropriately transcribed in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) embryos maintained high LIN-15B levels in embryonic PGCs.
source: We found that, in contrast to wild-type, nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) embryos maintained high LIN-15B levels in embryonic PGCs (Figure 6B Right panels).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Zygotic expression of LIN-15B in PGCs is not activated in embryogenesis in either wild-type or nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) embryos.
source: In both cases, we observed strong GFP expression in somatic cells, but no expression in PGCs during embryogenesis (data not shown), indicating that zygotic expression of LIN-15B in PGCs is not activated in embryogenesis in either wild-type or nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) embryos.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of a lin-15B transcriptional reporter.

claim: In wild-type, zygotic expression of the lin-15B transcriptional reporter was first observed in the germline of L4 stage animals, in germ cells that have initiated oogenesis.
source: In wild-type, we first observed zygotic expression of the lin-15B transcriptional reporter in the germline of L4 stage animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), in germ cells that have initiated oogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of a lin-15B transcriptional reporter shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In animals derived from nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) mothers, zygotic expression of the lin-15B transcriptional reporter could be detected as early as the L1 stage in PGCs and their descendants.
source: In contrast, in animals derived from nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) mothers, zygotic expression of the lin-15B transcriptional reporter could be detected as early as the L1 stage in PGCs and their descendants (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of a lin-15B transcriptional reporter shown in Figure 6C.

claim: nos-1nos-2 activity is required both to promote the turnover of maternal LIN-15B in PGCs during embryonic development and to prevent premature zygotic transcription of the lin-15B locus in PGCs in the L1 stage.
source: We conclude that nos-1nos-2 activity is required both to promote the turnover of maternal LIN-15B in PGCs during embryonic development and to prevent premature zygotic transcription of the lin-15B locus in PGCs in the L1 stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from immunostaining and reporter analysis.

claim: Loss of maternal lin-15B was sufficient to fully suppress nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) sterility, even in the presence of one zygotic copy of lin-15B.
source: We found that loss of maternal lin-15B was sufficient to fully suppress nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) sterility, even in the presence of one zygotic copy of lin-15B (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The penetrance of the suppression of nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) sterility was dependent on the dosage of maternal lin-15B.
source: The penetrance of the suppression was dependent on the dosage of maternal lin-15B.
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis.

claim: nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) animals with only one copy of maternal lin-15B were only 32% sterile compared to 70% sterility for animals with two copies of maternal lin-15B and 0% with animals with zero copies of maternal lin-15B.
source: nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) animals with only one copy of maternal lin-15B were only 32% sterile compared to 70% sterility for animals with two copies of maternal lin-15B and 0% with animals with zero copies of maternal lin-15B (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Maternal lin-15B is primarily responsible for the sterility of nos-1nos-2 animals, although zygotic Lin-15B activity may also contribute.
source: We conclude that maternal lin-15B is primarily responsible for the sterility of nos-1nos-2 animals, although zygotic Lin-15B activity may also contribute.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from genetic dosage experiments.

claim: Loss of lin-15B reduced gene misexpression in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs.
source: We found that loss of lin-15B reduced gene misexpression in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Of the 1430 upregulated genes in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs, 31% (452) had significantly lower expression levels in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi);lin-15B(RNAi) PGCs.
source: Of the 1430 upregulated genes in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs, 31% (452) had significantly lower expression levels in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi);lin-15B(RNAi) PGCs (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Ectopic lin-15B activity is responsible for a significant number of misexpressed genes in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs.
source: These data indicate that ectopic lin-15B activity is responsible for a significant number of misexpressed genes in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi) PGCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from RNA-seq data comparing double and triple mutants.

claim: Loss of lin-15B does not rescue the delay in maternal mRNA turnover observed in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) PGCs.
source: We found that the turnover of mex-5 and C01G8.1 mRNAs was still delayed in these embryos, as is observed in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). We conclude that loss of lin-15B does not rescue the delay in maternal mRNA turnover observed in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) PGCs.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: utx-1 transcripts are rare in wild-type PGCs (FPKM <0.2) and are overexpressed 9.1-fold in mes-2(RNAi) PGCs.
source: Like other X-linked genes, utx-1 transcripts are rare in wild-type PGCs (FPKM <0.2) (Supplementary file 4) and are overexpressed 9.1-fold in mes-2(RNAi) PGCs.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: In nos-1(gv5) nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs, the utx-1 locus acquires a new ATAC-seq peak and utx-1 transcripts are overexpressed 160-fold.
source: In nos-1(gv5) nos-2(RNAi) L1 PGCs, the utx-1 locus acquires a new ATAC-seq peak (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and utx-1 transcripts are overexpressed 160-fold.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: utx-1 overexpression was reduced significantly by 2.4-fold in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi);lin-15B(RNAi) PGCs.
source: This overexpression was reduced significantly by 2.4-fold in nos-1(gv5)nos-2(RNAi);lin-15B(RNAi) PGCs.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Reduction of utx-1 activity by RNAi partially suppressed nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) sterility.
source: Consistent with this prediction, we found that reduction of utx-1 activity by RNAi partially suppressed nos-1(gv5)nos-2(ax3103) sterility (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activation of utx-1 may participate in a regulatory loop downstream of maternal LIN-15B that further weakens mes activity in nos-1nos-2 animals.
source: These results suggest that activation of utx-1 may participate in a regulatory loop downstream of maternal LIN-15B that further weakens mes activity in nos-1nos-2 animals.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the genetic and expression data.

claim: PGCs lacking Nanos overexpress hundreds of transcripts normally expressed in oocytes due to both delayed turn-over of maternal mRNAs and inappropriate transcription of genes normally silent in PGCs.
source: In this study, we have examined the transcriptome of PGCs lacking Nanos function in C. elegans. We have found that PGCs lacking Nanos overexpress 100 s of transcripts normally expressed in oocytes. Our observations indicate that this defect is due to both delayed turn-over of maternal mRNAs and inappropriate transcription of genes normally silent in PGCs, including oocyte genes.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the experimental data.

claim: LIN-15B is a critical maternally-inherited factor that must be turned-over by Nanos in PGCs to prevent inappropriate transcription.
source: We identify LIN-15B as a critical maternally-inherited factor that must be turned-over by Nanos in PGCs to prevent inappropriate transcription.
evidence: This is a main conclusion supported by genetic and expression data.

claim: Clearing of maternal LIN-15B by Nanos allows the PRC2/MES-4 network of chromatin modifiers to reprogram PGCs away from an inherited (maternal) oocyte program to a pregametic germ cell program.
source: We propose that clearing of maternal LIN-15B by Nanos allows the PRC2/MES-4 network of chromatin modifiers to reprogram PGCs away from an inherited (maternal) oocyte program to a pregametic germ cell program.
evidence: This is the main model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Nanos facilitates the maternal-to-zygotic transition in PGCs by accelerating the turnover of maternal mRNAs.
source: Our findings suggest that Nanos facilitates this transition in PGCs by accelerating the turnover of maternal mRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on maternal mRNA turnover.

claim: Nanos family members are thought to silence mRNAs by interacting with the sequence-specific RNA-binding protein Pumilio and with the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex.
source: Nanos family members are thought to silence mRNAs by interacting with the sequence-specific RNA-binding protein Pumilio and with the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex, which interferes with translation and can also destabilize RNAs. (Lai et al., 2012a; Suzuki et al., 2012; Swartz et al., 2014; Wharton et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depletion of five Pumilio-like proteins (fbf-1, fbf-2, puf-6, puf-7 and puf-8) phenocopies the nos-1nos-2 PGC phenotypes.
source: Depletion of five of these (fbf-1, fbf-2, puf-6, puf-7 and puf-8) phenocopies the nos-1nos-2 PGC phenotypes, including failure to incorporate in the somatic gonad, premature proliferation, and eventually cell death (Subramaniam and Seydoux, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: NOS-1 and NOS-2 function with Pumilio-like proteins to repress the translation of certain maternal RNAs.
source: These observations suggest that NOS-1 and NOS-2 function with Pumilio-like proteins to repress the translation of certain maternal RNAs.
evidence: This is an inference from genetic observations.

claim: In sea urchins, Nanos silences the mRNA coding for the CNOT6 deadenylase, which indirectly stabilizes other maternal mRNAs.
source: Paradoxically, in sea urchins, Nanos silences the mRNA coding for the CNOT6 deadenylase, which indirectly stabilizes other maternal mRNAs (Swartz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In sea urchins, Nanos was found to silence eEF1A expression, leading to a transient period of translational quiescence in PGCs.
source: In that system, Nanos was also found to silence eEF1A expression, leading to a transient period of translational quiescence in PGCs (Oulhen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Elimination of maternal LIN-15B restores fertility to nos-1nos-2 mutants and lessens the upregulation of many misregulated genes.
source: Two lines of evidence indicate that LIN-15B is responsible for much of the abnormal gene expression observed in nos-1nos-2 PGCs by the first larval stage. First, elimination of maternal LIN-15B restores fertility to nos-1nos-2 mutants and lessens the upregulation of many misregulated genes (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by genetic and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6.

claim: LIN-15B is a known genetic antagonist of MES function in somatic cells.
source: Second, LIN-15B is a known genetic antagonist of MES function in somatic cells (Petrella et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2005), and PGCs lacking mes activity upregulate many of the same genes upregulated in nos-1nos-2 PGCs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PGCs lacking mes activity upregulate many of the same genes upregulated in nos-1nos-2 PGCs, with the strongest correlation seen for genes on the X chromosome.
source: Second, LIN-15B is a known genetic antagonist of MES function in somatic cells (Petrella et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2005), and PGCs lacking mes activity upregulate many of the same genes upregulated in nos-1nos-2 PGCs. The strongest correlation is seen for genes on the X chromosome (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), a well-documented focus of MES-dependent silencing (Bender et al., 2006; Garvin et al., 1998; Gaydos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Failure to downregulate maternal LIN-15B interferes with MES-dependent reprogramming of PGC chromatin and is the primary cause of PGC death in Nanos mutants.
source: Together these findings indicate that failure to downregulate maternal LIN-15B interferes with MES-dependent reprogramming of PGC chromatin and is the primary cause of PGC death in Nanos mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and expression data.

claim: Maternal LIN-15B may potentiate zygotic lin-15B expression as MES-dependent silencing of the X-chromosome becomes compromised.
source: The lin-15B locus is on the X chromosome and is ectopically transcribed in nos-1nos-2 PGCs at hatching. These observations raise the possibility that maternal LIN-15B potentiates zygotic lin-15B expression as MES-dependent silencing of the X-chromosome becomes compromised.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the data.

claim: utx-1 encodes a de-methylase that removes the silencing mark deposited by the PRC2 complex.
source: utx-1 encodes a de-methylase that removes the silencing mark deposited by the PRC2 complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about UTX-1 function.

claim: Upregulation of utx-1 was shown recently to promote reprogramming of adult germline stem cells into neurons.
source: Upregulation of utx-1 was shown recently to promote reprogramming of adult germline stem cells into neurons (Seelk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: utx-1 may oppose MES activity directly by removing the silencing mark deposited by the PRC2 complex.
source: utx-1 encodes a de-methylase that removes the silencing mark deposited by the PRC2 complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of UTX-1 and its upregulation in nos-1nos-2 mutants.

claim: nos-2 was shown to function redundantly with xnd-1 to repress histone active marks in PGCs.
source: Recently, nos-2 was shown to function redundantly with xnd-1 to repress histone active marks in PGCs (Mainpal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: XND-1 is a chromatin-associated protein expressed in PGCs throughout embryogenesis.
source: XND-1 is a chromatin-associated protein expressed in PGCs throughout embryogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: XND-1 may directly activate MES-dependent remodeling in PGCs.
source: An exciting possibility is that XND-1 directly activates MES-dependent remodeling in PGCs.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Nanos could promote germ cell fate by eliminating any maternal factors that would interfere with MES-dependent chromatin remodeling.
source: In that context, Nanos could promote germ cell fate simply by eliminating any maternal factors that would interfere with that remodeling.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the findings.

claim: Nanos accelerates the turn-over of several maternal mRNAs coding for transcription factors that function in somatic embryonic lineages, including pha-4, hlh-1 and tbx-2.
source: In addition to LIN-15B, we have found that Nanos accelerates the turn-over of several maternal mRNAs coding for transcription factors that function in somatic embryonic lineages, including pha-4, hlh-1 and tbx-2 (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Perdurance of somatic transcription factors contributes to the complex transcriptional profile of nos-1nos-2 PGCs.
source: We speculate that perdurance of these somatic transcription factors contributes to the complex transcriptional profile of nos-1nos-2 PGCs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the data.

claim: The primary function of Nanos may be to clear the PGCs of any mRNAs that promote somatic development.
source: The primary function of Nanos may be, therefore, to clear the PGCs of any mRNAs that promote somatic development.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Previous studies in Drosophila and Xenopus reported the expression of somatic transcripts in PGCs lacking Nanos.
source: This interpretation is consistent with previous studies in Drosophila and Xenopus that reported the expression of somatic transcripts in PGCs lacking Nanos (Deshpande et al., 1999b; Hayashi et al., 2004; Kadyrova et al., 2007; Lai et al., 2012b; Oulhen et al., 2017; Swartz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In PGCs, Nanos opposes LIN-15B and DRM transcription factors.
source: Our genetic findings indicate that, in PGCs, Nanos opposes LIN-15B and DRM transcription factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the genetic suppression experiments.

claim: In somatic cells, DRM transcription factors silence Nanos.
source: Studies in Drosophila and mammals have reported that, in somatic cells, the reverse is true: DRM transcription factors silence Nanos.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of the DRM subunit lethal (3) malignant brain tumor [l(3)mbt] leads to tumorous growth in Drosophila imaginal disks and ectopic expression of germline genes, including nanos.
source: Loss of the DRM subunit lethal (3) malignant brain tumor [l(3)mbt] leads to tumorous growth in Drosophila imaginal disks and ectopic expression of germline genes, including nanos (Janic et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of the retinoblastoma transcription factor (Rb) leads to activation of nanos transcription in mammalian tissue culture cells and in Drosophila wings.
source: Similarly, loss of the retinoblastoma transcription factor (Rb) leads to activation of nanos transcription in mammalian tissue culture cells and in Drosophila wings, which in turn is thought to repress the translation of Rb targets (Miles and Dyson, 2014; Miles et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A complex regulatory feedback loop has been reported between the LSD1 demethylase and the Nanos partner Pumilio in Drosophila and human bladder carcinoma cells.
source: A complex regulatory feedback loop has also been reported between the LSD1 demethylase and the Nanos partner Pumilio in Drosophila and human bladder carcinoma cells (Miles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Nanos functions in an ancient transcriptional/post-transcriptional regulatory switch that controls gene expression during development.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that Nanos functions in an ancient transcriptional/post-transcriptional regulatory switch that controls gene expression during development.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on multiple studies.
